title: Match cuts
sourceNote: Seamless Storytelling: The Power of Match Cuts in Animation, Jacob Richardson and Ryan Plummer
summary: Join two shots through shared movement, shape, color, or sound.

overview.purpose: A match cut joins two scenes through something they share, so the jump reads as one continuous move.
overview.when: Planning or animating a transition between two scenes, shots, or objects in motion design, video, or UI animation.
takeaways: Match movement, shape, color, or sound
Lock position, scale, and angle at the cut
Continue the move on the next frame
The match has to mean something

sections.title: Prompt
sections.intro: Paste this when you brief a transition.
sections.text: Use when planning or animating a transition between two scenes, shots, or objects in motion design, video, or UI animation, and the change should feel continuous through matched movement, framing or shape, color, or sound. A match cut joins two scenes through something they share. The viewer’s mind completes the jump, so the cut feels natural, and you skip a hard morph. Source: School of Motion, “Seamless Storytelling: The Power of Match Cuts in Animation,” Jacob Richardson and Ryan Plummer. https://schoolofmotion.com/blog/match-cuts

sections.title: When to use
sections.intro: Use a match cut when the change should feel continuous.

items.title: Skip the morph
items.more: A coin becomes a planet, a wheel becomes a clock. The cut does the transforming.

items.title: Time passing
items.more: The match holds the subject while time moves.

items.title: Symbolism
items.more: The shared trait is the point, not only the trick.

items.title: Between scenes
items.text: Move smoothly, and steer the eye.
items.more: The cut places the viewer’s look for the next shot.

sections.title: Match types
sections.intro: Pick the strongest thing the two shots share.

items.title: Movement
items.text: Trajectory, speed, and direction carry across.
items.more: Spins, position changes, and scale-ups or scale-downs all work.

items.title: Framing or shape
items.text: Similar shapes sit in the same spot, at about the same size.
items.more: Composition comes first. Keep one constant focal element as the anchor.

items.title: Color
items.text: A dominant color carries from A to B.
items.more: A color block is enough when it is what the eye is on.

items.title: Sound
items.text: A continuing sound bridges the cut.
items.more: An audio cue can sell a visual match too.

sections.title: Steps
sections.intro: Find the overlap, then lock the frame where the cut happens.

tutorials.title: Build the cut
steps: Find the shared trait. List each subject’s shape, motion, color, and sound, and pick the strongest overlap. If nothing overlaps, add one, for example by reshaping or recoloring B to echo A.
Lock the position. Put B at the same screen position, scale, and angle as A at the cut frame. Line up their centers of mass, or the focal point.

Keep the momentum. Plan one continuous move across both shots. Cut mid-move and start B on the next frame. In a 12-frame move, cut on frame 6 and pick up B on frame 7. Never restart the easing, and keep the direction and speed.
Guide the eye. Where the viewer looks at the end of A is where the key action starts in B. Use geometry, motion paths, and contrast.
Add sound. Put a whoosh, a hit, or a continuous tone on the cut.
Check it. Watch at full speed, then frame by frame around the cut.

sections.title: Before you ship
sections.intro: Watch it at full speed, then frame by frame around the cut.
items: Position, scale, and angle line up, so the eye doesn’t jump
Direction and speed carry through, with no stall, reset, or double frame
One clear focal element on each side of the cut
The match means something: symbolism, time passing, or the story moving forward
Sound supports the cut, or at least doesn’t fight it
A first-time viewer reads it as a continuation

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.intro: If the eye jumps, the match failed.

items.title: Subject is offset
items.text: Re-align B to A’s position and scale at the cut frame.
items.more: The eye jumps when B does not sit where A left off.

items.title: Motion stutters
items.text: Continue on the next frame of the same move.
items.more: Don’t restart the easing at the cut.

items.title: Too subtle to read
items.text: Make the shared shape or color dominant.

items.title: Too many in a row
items.text: Save them for moments that carry meaning.

items.title: Shapes too different
items.more: Or add a quick blur or scale to hide the gap.
